strapline: Solwezi sends the sedition case to the High Court, a scuffle at the Supreme Court, a seat on the rights council — and four goals in Ndola

stories.title: ‘No jurisdiction’: Solwezi sends the Mundubile and Zulu sedition case to the High Court — and the question of a Lusaka hearing is left for the judges
stories.excerpt: Principal Resident Magistrate Mambwe Mukonde ruled on Tuesday 13 October that the Solwezi Magistrates’ Court cannot hear the two-count sedition case against Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu, and referred it to the High Court. The State had not disputed the defence’s claim that the alleged offences took place in Lusaka. No High Court date has been set, the two men have still not taken plea, and the separate treason matter is untouched. In Lusaka, a bench warrant was issued for Binwell Mpundu in his own sedition case.

image.label: Solwezi declines
image.caption: The Solwezi Magistrates’ Court has ruled that it has no jurisdiction over the sedition case against Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu; the matter now goes to the High Court.

body: The three-week argument over where Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu should answer sedition charges ended on Tuesday 13 October with a ruling that the court in Solwezi was never the right place to hear them. Principal Resident Magistrate Mambwe Mukonde held that the Subordinate Court lacked jurisdiction over the two-count case and referred it to the High Court, according to reports by Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer.

Citing the Subordinate Courts Act, the magistrate found that jurisdiction over the matter lay with the High Court. She noted that the State had not disputed the contents of the two accused men’s warn-and-caution statements, nor the defence’s assertion that the alleged offences were committed in Lusaka. She added that it was not within her authority to decide whether the case should be heard in Lusaka — a question the High Court will now have to settle for itself.

Mr Mundubile, the NRPUP’s presidential candidate at the 13 August general election, and Mr Zulu, his running mate, first appeared in Solwezi on 25 September, when plea was deferred because their lawyers could not attend, the Zambian Observer reported. On 5 October defence lawyer Bonaventure Mutale challenged the court’s jurisdiction, arguing that the alleged offences had occurred in the capital, and asked that the accused be allowed to give oral evidence in support of the objection, citing access to witnesses and the cost of travel.

Director of Public Prosecutions Gilbert Phiri opposed that application, arguing that it had no legal basis and that the points were already covered by documentary evidence, including the warn-and-caution statements. On 6 October the magistrate refused the request for oral evidence and reserved her ruling on jurisdiction for 13 October.

The charges, according to the Zambian Observer, arise from statements allegedly posted on Facebook after the election, including claims based on the NRPUP’s parallel vote tabulation that Mr Mundubile had won the presidency. Neither man has taken plea, and Tuesday’s ruling does not touch the merits: it decides only where the case will be heard, not whether the allegations are made out. Neither man has been convicted of anything.

No High Court hearing date has been confirmed. The two men also face separate treason allegations arising from the security investigation that followed the election; according to the Zambian Observer they were first arrested on 27 August and have remained in detention since. Tuesday’s ruling changes nothing in that matter, and it does not of itself determine whether the sedition case will be heard in Lusaka or elsewhere.

The sedition docket moved elsewhere on Tuesday too. At the Lusaka Magistrates’ Court, Magistrate Webster Milumbe issued a bench warrant for Binwell Mpundu, the former Nkana MP, after he failed to appear for his own sedition case, Zambia Monitor reported. The warrant is returnable on 2 November, when his two sureties are expected to explain his whereabouts. No statement from Mr Mpundu or his lawyers on Tuesday’s non-appearance has been reported.

That the DPP had opposed oral evidence and the magistrate refused it on 6 October. That a bench warrant for Binwell Mpundu is returnable on 2 November (Zambia Monitor).

stories.title: A scuffle on the Supreme Court steps: the Chief Justice tightens security after Davies Mwila is pushed to the ground — and the UPND condemns the attack while disputing the blame
stories.excerpt: Former PF secretary-general Davies Mwila was pushed to the ground outside the Supreme Court on Tuesday 13 October after a hearing in the Lima election petition. Chief Justice Mumba Malila called it an attack on the administration of justice and said security had been heightened. The UPND condemned the assault and dared a PF-Pamodzi youth official who blamed its cadres to produce evidence. Police have named no suspects.

image.label: Outside the Supreme Court
image.caption: The Judiciary says security has been heightened after former PF secretary-general Davies Mwila was pushed to the ground on the Supreme Court grounds on Tuesday 13 October.

body: An election petition hearing ended in a scuffle on Tuesday 13 October, when former Patriotic Front secretary-general Davies Mwila was pushed to the ground on the grounds of the Supreme Court in Lusaka. Video circulated by the Zambian Observer shows him struggling to get back to his feet as a group of people surrounds him. By evening the Chief Justice, the ruling party and Mr Mwila himself had all issued statements — and they do not agree on who was responsible.

Mr Mwila had attended the hearing of the Lima constituency petition in solidarity with Kelvin Kaunda, the NRPUP candidate who won the seat with 22,760 votes against 8,041 for the UPND’s Lee Mukupa, who is challenging the result, Zambia Monitor reported. According to the same report, the incident followed a confrontation with people Mr Mwila identified as UPND supporters, after proceedings had been adjourned; he is said to have mocked their ‘salt sana’ slogan by remarking that they were hungry. No injuries have been reported.

Chief Justice Mumba Malila condemned the incident in a statement on Tuesday as an attack on the administration of justice and on the integrity of the Judiciary. He said security at the courts had been heightened, that law-enforcement agencies were investigating and that those responsible would face the full force of the law.

body.text: Unruly conduct and violence will not be tolerated under any circumstances.
body.attribution: Chief Justice Mumba Malila, in a statement issued on Tuesday 13 October, as reported by Zambia Monitor

body: Given Gift Chibale, a PF-Pamodzi Alliance national youth official, publicly blamed suspected UPND cadres for the attack, Lusaka Times reported. The UPND Media Team condemned the assault in a statement of its own on Tuesday, said no political disagreement could justify physical attacks, and urged law enforcement to investigate professionally and impartially — but it also rejected the attribution. ‘An allegation does not become a fact simply because it is repeated publicly or attached to the name of a political party,’ the party said, adding that it intended to report Mr Chibale to the police under cybercrime laws.

Mr Mwila, for his part, said he had remained calm and had not assaulted anyone, and described himself as a senior citizen who deserved to be treated with dignity. He has given those involved a month to apologise. ‘I have given the people who attacked me one month to come and apologise because I have not hurt anyone,’ he said, as quoted by the Zambian Observer, urging those responsible to report themselves to the police.

The police have not named any suspects and no arrests have been reported. Both the UPND’s denial and Mr Chibale’s accusation remain unverified claims; the Judiciary’s statement does not attribute the assault to any party. The Lima petition itself continues, with no date for its next sitting reported in the pieces cited here.

stories.title: A seat without a contest: Zambia joins the UN Human Rights Council for 2027–2029 — as Human Rights Watch calls the uncontested vote ‘a mockery’
stories.excerpt: The UN General Assembly elected Zambia to the 47-member Human Rights Council on Tuesday 13 October, alongside Ghana, Nigeria and Burundi for Africa. Foreign Minister Mulambo Haimbe called it a milestone and thanked the states that backed the bid. Every regional group had put forward exactly as many candidates as seats, for the second year running, and Human Rights Watch said that made the word ‘election’ a mockery.

image.label: A seat in the Council
image.caption: Zambia will sit on the UN Human Rights Council from 2027 to 2029 after an uncontested vote in the General Assembly on Tuesday 13 October.

body: Zambia has won a three-year seat on the United Nations Human Rights Council. The General Assembly elected 15 members on Tuesday 13 October in New York, during its 81st session, and Zambia was among the four African states chosen, alongside Ghana, Nigeria and Burundi, Al Jazeera reported. The term runs from 2027 to 2029.

Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Minister Mulambo Haimbe, who led the delegation during the campaign, announced the result and described the election as a milestone in Zambia’s multilateral diplomacy, Lusaka Times reported. He said the seat offered what he called ‘two-way impact’: stronger protection of rights at home and a Council that better serves developing nations. In a statement carried by Lusaka Times and Open Zambia, the Government said it ‘expresses its sincere appreciation to all United Nations Member States that supported Zambia’s candidature’ and looked forward to working with the international community.

The Ministry’s statement tied the bid to the abolition of the death penalty, stronger protections for women, children and persons with disabilities, and wider access to education and social support, and linked all of it to President Hakainde Hichilema’s Grow Zambia Agenda. Zambia’s stated priorities for its term are the rights of women, children and vulnerable groups, the right to development, and the connection between human rights, climate resilience and sustainable development.

The 15 seats were filled without a contest. Each regional group nominated exactly as many candidates as it had seats — for the second year running, according to Al Jazeera. Asia-Pacific sent Kuwait, Nepal, Jordan and Japan; Latin America and the Caribbean sent Brazil, the Dominican Republic and Uruguay; Ireland and Germany took the Western seats and Moldova and Ukraine the Eastern European ones.

body.text: This uncompetitive vote makes a mockery of the word ‘election’.
body.attribution: Louis Charbonneau, UN director at Human Rights Watch, as reported by Al Jazeera on 14 October

body: Mr Charbonneau urged member states to insist on competitive slates so that candidates with poor human-rights records could be rejected, and said no one should have a seat on the body ‘handed to them on a silver platter’. The Al Jazeera report does not single out any elected state by name. UN spokesman Stephane Dujarric said the matter was one for the 193 member states, and that elected members carried ‘an added responsibility to protect human rights’.

The Council reviews countries’ rights records, appoints investigators and sends fact-finding missions. For Zambia the seat arrives in the same week that a sedition case against the opposition’s presidential candidate was referred to the High Court and a former ruling-party official was pushed to the ground outside the Supreme Court — both reported elsewhere in this edition — and it will mean a term of scrutiny as well as influence. The Government’s statement did not address the domestic arguments; it presented the seat as recognition of reforms already made.

stories.title: The steepest fall in the region — and the heaviest interest bill: Moody’s on Zambia’s debt, as Musokotwane takes the case to Bangkok
stories.excerpt: Moody’s projects that Zambia and Ethiopia will record the largest reductions in government debt in sub-Saharan Africa, and lists Zambia among eight countries with a positive outlook — while also forecasting that about 35 percent of its revenue will go on interest in 2027, the heaviest burden in the region alongside Kenya. State House called the projection the result of ‘hard choices’. The Finance Minister is now at the IMF–World Bank meetings in Bangkok, where he spoke for African borrowers on Tuesday.

image.label: Debt, falling
image.caption: Moody’s expects Zambia’s government debt to fall faster than almost any other in sub-Saharan Africa; the interest bill, it says, will stay the region’s heaviest.

body: Zambia’s government debt is set to fall further than almost any other in sub-Saharan Africa, Moody’s Ratings says — and its interest bill is set to remain the heaviest. The two findings sit side by side in the agency’s regional outlook, published on Wednesday 7 October and reported by Reuters, which raised its view of the region to positive, crediting reforms, strong commodity prices and easier access to financing.

Moody’s expects Zambia and Ethiopia to record the biggest drops in government debt in the region, and places Zambia among eight countries with a positive outlook, with South Africa, Namibia, Angola, Nigeria, Togo, Ghana and the Republic of Congo. Across the region it sees debt levelling off at 56.6 percent of GDP in 2027, down from 62.4 percent in 2025, and growth of 4.3 percent in both 2026 and 2027. But it also forecasts that around 35 percent of Zambia’s government revenue will go to interest payments in 2027 — the highest share in sub-Saharan Africa, matched only by Kenya.

State House welcomed the projection in a statement on Monday 12 October. Clayson Hamasaka, the Chief Communications Specialist, said the country’s debt was ‘set to fall further than almost anywhere else in the region’ and that this was ‘the result of hard choices, taken together, and of the patience and sacrifice of the Zambian people’, CAJ News and News Diggers reported. He added that the Government was not complacent — ‘the cost of servicing our debt remains too high’ — and said it would hold to fiscal discipline under the new IMF programme agreed at staff level on 9 October.

body.text: Bangkok: the delegation and the agenda

body: The arguments move this week to Bangkok, where the IMF and World Bank Group annual meetings run until Sunday 18 October — the first time in three years they have been held outside Washington. Finance and National Planning Minister Dr Situmbeko Musokotwane leads a delegation that includes Secretary to the Treasury Felix Nkulukusa, Bank of Zambia Governor Dr Denny Kalyalya and the permanent secretaries for energy and mines, Arnold Simwaba and Hapenga Kabeta, Lusaka Times reported.

According to a statement from the Office of the Secretary to the Treasury carried by Lusaka Times, the delegation will work to advance the proposed 36-month, US$1.47 billion Extended Credit Facility, including its reforms and prior actions, and meet IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva and World Bank President Ajay Banga. Also on the list: talks with the US Treasury, with Africa50 on financing for the Angola–Zambia power interconnector, the Kazungula Bridge corridor and domestic transmission, with partners on the Lobito Corridor, and with Standard Bank, Standard Chartered, Citi and J.P. Morgan.

On Tuesday 13 October Dr Musokotwane spoke for the Platform’s African members at the inaugural Governing Council meeting of the Borrowers’ Platform, a 31-member grouping of developing countries launched in Washington in April, Zambia Monitor reported. He argued that low-income borrowers should have a greater say in shaping the international debt system, that high financing costs and drawn-out restructurings were eating into development spending, and that the Platform should move ‘from establishing structures to delivering practical results’.

body.text: Decisions about debt therefore matter not only to governments, but also to the everyday lives of our people.
body.attribution: Dr Situmbeko Musokotwane, Finance and National Planning Minister, at the Borrowers’ Platform Governing Council in Bangkok on Tuesday 13 October, as reported by Zambia Monitor

stories.title: ‘Not reduced’: State House says CDF stays at K40 million and only the disbursements have changed — as the Treasury releases K806 million for schools
stories.excerpt: After the Finance Minister said next year’s Constituency Development Fund would fall below budget, State House said the allocation ‘has not been reduced and remains at 40 million kwacha per constituency’, with disbursements realigned to need and absorption. NRPUP’s Stephen Kampyongo says any cut will leave MPs unable to meet expectations the Government itself raised. Separately, the Treasury released K806.1 million in fourth-quarter school grants, completing more than K2.3 billion for 2026.

image.label: K40 million, realigned
image.caption: State House says the Constituency Development Fund remains K40 million per constituency; what has changed, it says, is how and when the money is released.

body: The Constituency Development Fund has not been cut, State House said in a statement reported on Tuesday 13 October — only the way it is paid out. The clarification came after Finance and National Planning Minister Dr Situmbeko Musokotwane had said that the 2027 allocation would be lower than initially budgeted, as the Treasury worked to contain this year’s overspend, and that the Food Reserve Agency would receive no Treasury money next season because it had bought more maize than was budgeted.

Clayson Hamasaka, State House Chief Communications Specialist, said the CDF allocation ‘has not been reduced and remains at 40 million kwacha per constituency’, the Zambian Observer reported. What the Government had done, he said, was realign disbursements according to each constituency’s needs and its ‘rate of absorption’. News Diggers carried the same message: the fund stands at K40 million, with releases adjusted to need.

body.text: The FRA stays in the market

body: Mr Hamasaka also said the FRA would continue to buy maize for the national strategic reserve next marketing season, in line with its mandate, and that the proposed changes did not mean the agency was leaving maize purchases altogether. The FRA, he said, was never created as a crop marketing agency; the Government intends to set up a dedicated crop marketing entity with private-sector participation to find export markets for surplus maize, as part of a Grow Zambia Agenda target of ten million tonnes.

The two statements are not easy to reconcile in full. Dr Musokotwane spoke of a 2027 allocation below what was budgeted, with councils to be informed; Mr Hamasaka speaks of an unchanged K40 million with disbursements re-timed. Neither statement, as reported, gives the figure councils will actually receive in 2027. That will become clear only when the 2027 Budget is tabled.

Stephen Kampyongo, the NRPUP MP for Shiwang’andu and a former Home Affairs Minister, said in an interview on Monday that a cut would make it hard for MPs to meet the public’s expectations, which he said the UPND Government had itself raised through its promotion of the fund, News Diggers reported. He called the reduction unfortunate.

body.text: K806.1 million for the fourth quarter

body: In the same week, the Treasury released K806.1 million in school grants for the fourth quarter of 2026, in a statement issued through the Office of the Secretary to the Treasury on Monday and reported by Zambia Monitor and News Diggers. The release, made within the first two weeks of the quarter, completes the year’s provision of more than K2.3 billion for free education. The money goes through the Ministry of Education to government-supported public schools for school feeding, teaching and learning materials, learner support and infrastructure maintenance.

Dr Musokotwane directed accounting staff in schools to provide timely and accurate financial guidance and called strict compliance with public financial management regulations ‘mandatory and non-negotiable’, Zambia Monitor reported. Misapplication of funds, unauthorised spending and failure to account for public resources would not be accepted, he said; the Ministry added that the success of the grants would be measured by learning outcomes, not by the amounts disbursed.

stories.title: A truce over the tax ledger: ZRA halts penalties, certificate suspensions and debt recovery while migrated records are reconciled
stories.excerpt: After moving years of historical tax transactions from retired systems onto TaxOnline, the Zambia Revenue Authority says it will not impose penalties, suspend Tax Clearance Certificates or pursue debt recovery over unreconciled historical data while taxpayers check their accounts. Business associations had raised concerns about suspended certificates and the reliability of the migrated records. A technical working group has been set up; no end date for the reconciliation period has been given.

image.label: The migrated ledger
image.caption: The Zambia Revenue Authority has paused enforcement over historical records it moved to TaxOnline this month, while taxpayers reconcile their accounts.

body: The Zambia Revenue Authority has called a pause. During the reconciliation of historical tax records it moved onto its TaxOnline platform this month, the authority will not impose penalties, suspend Tax Clearance Certificates or pursue debt recovery arising from historical data that has not yet been reconciled, Commissioner-General Dingani Banda said in a statement issued on Tuesday 13 October and reported by Zambia Monitor.

The assurance follows a meeting between the ZRA and the country’s main business associations, which the Ecofin Agency dates to Monday 12 October. Participants included the Zambia Association of Manufacturers, whose president Mohammed Umar co-chaired the meeting, the Zambia Institute of Chartered Accountants, the Bankers Association of Zambia and the Economics Association of Zambia. They raised concerns about certificates that had already been suspended, the reliability of the migrated records, administrative difficulties, the timing of the migration and what they saw as insufficient consultation beforehand.

According to both reports, the ZRA completed the transfer of historical tax account transactions from decommissioned legacy systems to TaxOnline earlier in October — Ecofin gives the date as 6 October. The migrated records cover returns, payments, offsets, assessments, penalties, fines, interest and refunds, bringing historical and current transactions onto one platform. The authority says the migration created no new tax liabilities, but acknowledges that balances may have changed and that some transaction references may look unfamiliar to taxpayers.

body.text: This data migration will empower taxpayers to access information that supports the reconciliation of their tax accounts.
body.attribution: Dingani Banda, ZRA Commissioner-General, in a statement on Tuesday 13 October, as reported by Zambia Monitor

body.text: What taxpayers are asked to do

body: Taxpayers are asked to review their migrated records, reconcile their accounts and report any discrepancies through the established channels; migrated data will be reconciled with each taxpayer before it is posted to their account. Those whose Tax Clearance Certificates were suspended are told to reapply for reinstatement. The ZRA has also set up a dedicated technical working group to improve communication and resolve migration and reconciliation problems, and Mr Umar welcomed the authority’s engagement.

Separately, the Extended Voluntary Disclosure Scheme remains open until 31 December 2026: eligible taxpayers who settle their outstanding principal tax can receive a full waiver of accrued penalties and interest, Ecofin reports. The ZRA has not said when the reconciliation period will end, nor who sits on the working group — the two details businesses will want next.

body.title: In brief
items: Migration to TaxOnline completed — early October (Ecofin: 6 October)
Meeting with business associations — Monday 12 October

End of reconciliation period — not announced

stories.title: Back to their stations: the Ministry of Health sends 123 headquarters officers to their posts and orders a qualifications audit — as ZAMMSA starts hiring again
stories.excerpt: An internal assessment found 123 officers working at the Ministry of Health’s Lusaka headquarters under temporary arrangements, outside an approved establishment of 403 positions. Health Minister Roma Chilengi says they are being redirected to their substantive stations and that everyone left at headquarters will be assessed against professional benchmarks. ZAMMSA, whose entire workforce was dismissed, has advertised eight senior posts, and the Ministry says it is seeking cheaper financing for the sector.

image.label: Back to the stations
image.caption: The Ministry of Health says 123 officers found working at its headquarters under temporary arrangements are being returned to the stations where they are actually posted.

body: The Ministry of Health has begun what it calls an institutional clean-up of its Lusaka headquarters, sending 123 officers back to the stations where they are formally posted. An internal assessment found the officers had been working at headquarters under temporary administrative arrangements, outside the approved establishment, Zambia Monitor and News Diggers reported on Wednesday 14 October.

The 2021 establishment caps headquarters staffing at 403 positions, according to Zambia Monitor, and the 123 fell outside it. Health Minister Professor Roma Chilengi said in a statement on Tuesday 13 October that the officers were being returned to the stations where their pay points and original postings sit, and that the move was intended to strengthen delivery at frontline facilities and decentralised administrative centres.

body.text: An audit of everyone who remains

body: The redeployment is the first step. Professor Chilengi said the Ministry would now assess the qualifications and competencies of everyone holding one of the 403 headquarters positions; staff who lack the academic, professional or technical qualifications their roles require will be moved to operational stations that match their verified credentials.

body.text: Every position in the approved structure will be evaluated against established professional benchmarks and job descriptions.
body.attribution: Professor Roma Chilengi, Minister of Health, in a statement on Tuesday 13 October, as reported by Zambia Monitor

body: The Ministry describes the exercise as part of wider reforms to enforce structural compliance and improve service delivery. No deadline for the qualifications assessment has been given, and neither report carries a response from health workers’ unions.

The clean-up follows the Minister’s decision to dismiss the entire workforce of the Zambia Medicines and Medical Supplies Agency ‘in national interest’, citing years of repeated problems and the findings of a forensic audit commissioned by the Auditor General. ZAMMSA has now advertised eight vacancies — seven director-level positions and an executive secretary in the Director General’s office — seeking ‘suitably qualified and experienced Zambians’, News Diggers reported on Tuesday. Professor Chilengi has said the agency will need more than 400 employees to run its operations, so the eight posts are the start of a much longer rebuild.

body.text: The cost of borrowing for health

body: Money is the other front. At the third Health Sector Policy Meeting of the year, Dr George Sinyangwe, the Ministry’s Permanent Secretary for Donor Coordination, said the Government was exploring cheaper financing for the sector — lower-interest loans for institutions, debt-swap arrangements and a review of financing packages — noting that some entities faced borrowing costs of up to 30 percent against a prime lending rate of about 15 percent, Lusaka Times reported. Proposals for concessional loans and grants from multilateral development banks are being developed through the Health Impact Investment Platform with the World Health Organization. For the cooperating partners, Seth Broekman’s message, delivered through chairperson Anna Holmstrom, was that ‘Zambia must move beyond incremental improvements and implement transformative measures’ if universal health coverage is to be reached by 2030.

stories.title: ‘A matter concerning an individual’: the Government says clergy facing serious allegations should step aside — and the Green Party says the calls on Archbishop Banda are premature
stories.excerpt: Information Permanent Secretary Thabo Kawana, in a statement that named no cleric, said it was advisable for clergy facing serious allegations to step aside while the facts are established, and that a case against an individual is not an attack on the Church. The statement follows the arrest of Lusaka Archbishop Alick Banda, who is contesting a charge in court. Two MPs say he should not preside at Mass meanwhile; Green Party leader Peter Sinkamba says resignation calls are premature and politically motivated.

image.label: Church and state
image.caption: A Government statement says clergy facing serious allegations should consider stepping aside; the Green Party says calls for Archbishop Alick Banda to resign are premature.

body: The Government has set out, for the first time since the arrest of Lusaka Archbishop Alick Banda, a general position on what a cleric facing serious allegations should do: step aside. In a statement on Monday 12 October reported by Lusaka Times and News Diggers, Thabo Kawana, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Information and Media, said it was advisable for clergy facing serious allegations to consider stepping aside, taking leave or relinquishing responsibilities while the facts were established — a step he described as ‘not a new or unusual principle’ and one that did not imply guilt.

The statement named no one. Mr Kawana drew a line between the Church — ‘a respected faith community with a long history of spiritual guidance, social service and national contribution’ — and individual clergy, saying a case against a cleric was ‘a matter concerning an individual’ rather than an attack on the Church, and that no one was above the law. He cited Catholic, Anglican and evangelical examples of clergy stepping aside, and said the Government would respect the presumption of innocence and apply the law impartially.

Archbishop Banda was arrested on 28 September and charged by the Drug Enforcement Commission with possession of property reasonably suspected to have been unlawfully obtained, Lusaka Times reported; News Diggers says the arrest is linked to a Toyota Hilux suspected of having been unlawfully obtained from the Zambia Revenue Authority. The Archbishop is contesting the charge in court. He has not been convicted of anything, and the pieces cited here carry no statement from him or from the Archdiocese on the calls for him to step aside.

Dr Clement Andeleki, the MP for Kazungula North, said the Archbishop should not preside over Mass while the case was active, calling it ‘taboo’ for someone facing such serious charges to do so and citing the Pope’s acceptance of a San Diego bishop’s resignation after criminal charges, Lusaka Times reported. Nominated MP Noel Nkoma went further, accusing the Archbishop of embarrassing the Church and of portraying himself as a politician. Rufunsa MP Sheal Mulyata called the matter important but declined to comment further for now. The report notes that the three share the Archbishop’s faith.

Peter Sinkamba, leader of the Green Party, took the opposite view in a statement on Monday reported by Zambia Monitor. Calls for the Archbishop and other Catholic leaders to resign were premature and politically motivated, he said; automatic resignation on arrest would invite the political misuse of the justice system, could be read as an admission of guilt, and would weaken the Church’s role as a critic of state power. Under Canon 401, he argued, a bishop is urged to resign for ill health or another grave cause, and an arrest by the State does not automatically meet that standard — the Holy See can weigh any claim of persecution itself.

body.text: Ignoring calls for resignation preserves the prophetic voice of the Church.
body.attribution: Peter Sinkamba, Green Party leader, in a statement on Monday 12 October, as reported by Zambia Monitor

body: Mr Sinkamba said the Archbishop should ignore the calls, that those making them were exercising free speech, and that if the Government’s case had merit it should start the trial. News Diggers notes that the arrest drew condemnation from some Catholics and from critics of the Government, some of whom accused the State of fighting the Church — the charge Mr Kawana’s statement was plainly written to answer.

stories.title: Four goals and the road to Los Angeles reopens: the Copper Queens beat Uganda 4–1 in Ndola to go through 5–3 on aggregate — Ghana next, in February
stories.excerpt: Trailing 2–1 from Kampala, Zambia needed a performance at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium on Tuesday 13 October and produced one: Natasha Nanyangwe and Eneless Phiri scored inside 20 minutes, and Barbra Banda added two after the break for a 4–1 win and a 5–3 aggregate. Sylvia Kabene’s equaliser was Uganda’s only reply. The third round of the 2028 Olympic qualifiers brings Ghana, 10–0 aggregate winners over Mauritius, in February 2027.

image.label: Four in Ndola
image.caption: The Copper Queens overturned a first-leg deficit with a 4–1 win over Uganda at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium on Tuesday 13 October, advancing 5–3 on aggregate.

body: The Copper Queens asked for one more chance and took it. A 4–1 win over Uganda at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola on Tuesday 13 October overturned the 2–1 deficit from the first leg in Kampala and sent Zambia through to the third round of qualifying for the 2028 Olympic Games, 5–3 on aggregate, Lusaka Times and ZamFoot reported.

The start was everything. Natasha Nanyangwe headed in from a corner in the eighth minute to level the tie on aggregate. Uganda hit back almost at once — Sylvia Kabene equalised on the night in the 14th minute, and for a few minutes the Crested Cranes were ahead again overall. Then Eneless Phiri met a Prisca Chilufya cross in the 20th minute, and Zambia led on the night and were level in the tie.

Barbra Banda, whose finishing has carried this team through two Olympic campaigns, made the difference after the break. She scored in the 50th minute to put Zambia ahead on aggregate for the first time, and added a second late in the match — set up by Rachael Kundananji, according to ZamFoot — to make the result safe. The two reports differ on the exact minute of the fourth goal, so Lusaka Brief gives none.

body.text: We told Uganda that we will beat them at our home ground.
body.attribution: Rachael Kundananji, Copper Queens forward, after the match in Ndola on Tuesday 13 October, as quoted by Lusaka Times

body: The reward is a third-round tie against Ghana, who beat Mauritius 7–0 in their second leg to go through 10–0 on aggregate, in February 2027. Zambia played at the last two Olympic tournaments; a third in a row now depends on the Ghana tie and whatever follows it. On the evidence of Tuesday night the squad has depth as well as a star: the goals came from three different players, and Banda’s brace came when it was needed most.

stories.title: A winning start in Rabat: Zambia’s futsal side beat Libya 3–1 at the Africa Cup of Nations — the hosts, Morocco, are next
stories.excerpt: Royd Chishala scored in the second minute and Patrick Mwila added two as Zambia opened their fourth Futsal Africa Cup of Nations with a 3–1 win over Libya in Rabat on Monday 12 October. Mohammed Abu Raas pulled one back late on. Andrea Cristoforetti’s side, who went out in the group stage in 2024, now face hosts Morocco on Wednesday 14 October and Algeria on Friday 16 October.

image.label: Three in Rabat
image.caption: Zambia opened the CAF Futsal Africa Cup of Nations in Morocco with a 3–1 win over Libya on Monday 12 October; the hosts are next, on Wednesday.

body: Zambia’s futsal team have begun the TotalEnergies CAF Futsal Africa Cup of Nations in Morocco with a win. Royd Chishala scored inside two minutes and Patrick Mwila struck twice — once about four minutes later and again in the 23rd minute, straight after the restart — to put Zambia 3–0 up against Libya in Rabat on Monday 12 October, CAF reported. Mohammed Abu Raas pulled one back for Libya late in the game, and Zambia closed out a 3–1 victory in their Group A opener.

Mwila was named player of the match, according to Africa Top Sports, which also reported that Zambia’s ambassador to Morocco, Eliphas Chinyonga, was in the stands. The tournament runs from 12 to 21 October.

body.text: A fourth finals, and a tougher group

body: This is Zambia’s fourth appearance at the futsal finals, after 2008, 2016 and 2024, CAF’s tournament profile notes. Two years ago the team beat Ghana 5–2 but lost to Angola and the hosts, Morocco, and went out in the group stage with three points. Head coach Andrea Cristoforetti, in charge then too, is at his second consecutive finals and is credited by CAF with building a new generation of players. Zambia reached Morocco by beating Ghana over two legs in the qualifying play-offs.

Group A is not kind. Morocco, the hosts, are Zambia’s second opponents on Wednesday 14 October, with Algeria to follow on Friday 16 October; Libya meet Algeria on Wednesday and Morocco on Friday. Three points from the opening game give Cristoforetti’s side a platform: in 2024 the team finished the group stage with the same total.

analysis.title: What Solwezi decided — and what it left open
analysis.body: Tuesday’s ruling is narrower than either side’s supporters may read it. Magistrate Mukonde did not find the charges weak or the prosecution improper; she found that a Subordinate Court in Solwezi was not the forum, because the State never contested that the alleged acts happened in Lusaka. The defence won the point it argued, and the case now moves to the High Court. But she also declined to say where that court should sit, so the Lusaka question is still live. The State resisted the challenge; it may now argue the question of venue afresh. For the accused, the practical effect is weeks, not days: no High Court date exists, plea has still not been taken, and the treason detention runs on regardless. What to watch: the first High Court listing; whether the DPP seeks to keep the matter outside Lusaka; and how the detention question is handled alongside the sedition case.

analysis.title: Falling debt, rising interest: two Moody’s numbers that are both true
analysis.body: State House led with the flattering number, and it is real: Moody’s expects Zambia’s debt stock to fall faster than almost any in sub-Saharan Africa. The uncomfortable number sits in the same report. About 35 percent of government revenue will go on interest in 2027 — the heaviest burden in the region, shared with Kenya. Both follow from the same history. The restructuring reduced the stock of debt; the cost of what remains, and of the domestic borrowing that fills the gap, is what keeps the interest bill high. The Government’s case is that discipline under the new IMF programme brings the second number down behind the first. The sceptics’ case is that a Treasury already telling the FRA to expect no money next season has little room if interest stays that high. What to watch in Bangkok: whether the ‘prior actions’ for the US$1.47 billion facility are published, and what the commercial lenders on the delegation’s list are offered.

analysis.title: A seat in Geneva, earned without a vote
analysis.body: Zambia’s election to the Human Rights Council was a diplomatic success, and the Government is entitled to say so. It is also the second year in which every regional group filled its seats without a contest, which is why Human Rights Watch used the word ‘mockery’. Both things can be held at once. The case for the seat, as Lusaka made it, is a record of reform — the abolition of the death penalty, disability and child protection — and a promise to bring developing-country concerns to a body critics say is remote. The case against is not aimed at Zambia alone: that uncontested slates let any state through, and that membership now sits beside treason and sedition prosecutions of opposition figures that the Council’s own mechanisms may one day examine. A seat brings scrutiny with it. What to watch: how Zambia votes on country resolutions in its first session, and whether its envoys welcome or resist attention to the cases at home.
